From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

# Project Kestrel — Review of Seller's SPA Positions & Disclosure Letter

Below is my critical analysis for the buyer. I've worked through each position, identified where the Seller has reached for buyer-unfavourable terms, and flagged where the Disclosure Letter is doing work the Seller hopes we won't notice. Recommendations are summarised at the end.

---

## A. Liability architecture — several overreaches bundled together

### 1. Fundamental/title warranties caught by the general cap and 18-month limit (Clause 12 / "administrative simplicity")
This is the single most important issue. The Seller proposes that **capacity and title warranties** sit under the **same AUD 4.8m cap and 18-month notification window** as general warranties, dressed up as "administrative simplicity."

Reasoning: Title and capacity go to the root of what we are buying — the shares themselves. If title fails, we may have paid AUD 24m for nothing. Capping recovery at 20% of price and extinguishing claims at 18 months is wholly inappropriate for these. Market standard is:
- **Fundamental/title/capacity warranties capped at 100% of purchase price** (AUD 24m);
- **Longer limitation period** (typically 6–7 years, aligned with tax);
- Tax claims usually carried out to the statutory limitation period too.

**Push back hard.** Separate "Fundamental Warranties" (title, capacity, authority) capped at 100% of price, and carve tax out to at least the statute-barred period. This is non-negotiable.

### 2. General cap at 20% (AUD 4.8m)
A 20% cap is within market range but on the lower side for a private tech business with the risk profile here (concentration, IP, privacy incident). Given the specific unresolved matters below, I'd push for **30–50%** on general warranties, or at minimum ensure the specific risk items are handled by indemnities that sit **outside** the general cap.

### 3. Thresholds (Clause 12.2)
De minimis AUD 25k / basket AUD 250k with **excess-only** (tipping-above) recovery. The threshold levels are defensible, but note the Seller has chosen a **deductible/excess basket**, not a first-dollar basket. On a AUD 24m deal a AUD 250k basket (~1%) is acceptable; the structure is a negotiation point — push for first-dollar ("tip the basket") recovery.

### 4. "Any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" (Clause 12.3/13)
This is a **drafting trap**. It flips the default so that every limitation (cap, time bar, thresholds, exclusive remedy) silently swallows fundamental warranties, tax, indemnities and any specific indemnities we negotiate — unless we remember to carve each one out in every clause.

**Push back:** reverse the default. Limitations should apply to **general warranty claims only**, and specific indemnities, fundamental warranties, tax and fraud must be expressly excluded from the general regime. Also ensure **fraud/wilful concealment** is excluded from all caps and time limits (never accept a cap on fraud).

### 5. Exclusive remedy / non-reliance applying to "all Claims of any nature" (9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)
Combined with Clause 8.3 (below), the Seller is trying to build a closed system where our only recourse is a capped, time-barred warranty claim, and even that is undercut by the knowledge and disclosure provisions. Non-reliance clauses must always carve out **fraud and fraudulent misrepresentation**.

---

## B. Disclosure & knowledge — the Seller is shifting diligence risk onto us

### 6. General/"data room" disclosure (Schedule 7, Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2)
The Seller discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room" plus the Accounts, registers and **publicly searchable records**. This is a **sweep-up/deemed disclosure** against the warranties.

Reasoning: This means anything buried anywhere in the data room (or discoverable on any public register) is deemed disclosed and defeats a warranty claim, even if we never reasonably could have appreciated its significance.

**Push back:** disclosure should be **fair disclosure** — disclosed with sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter. Reject disclosure of "public records" generally. Consider whether certain known problem areas (privacy incident, Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay) should be dealt with by **specific indemnity** rather than left to disclosure at all.

### 7. Buyer knowledge wipe-out (Clause 8.3)
"No claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers **had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records**."

This is an aggressive **anti-sandbagging + constructive knowledge** clause. "Discoverable" imputes knowledge of anything we theoretically could have found. Combined with clause 6 and clause 7.1 of the Disclosure Letter, it eviscerates the warranties.

**Push back:** 
- Delete constructive/"discoverable" knowledge — limit to **actual knowledge** of named deal-team individuals, if we accept any knowledge qualifier at all;
- Buyer's preferred position is a **pro-sandbagging** clause: warranties survive regardless of buyer knowledge. At minimum, reject "discoverable."

### 8. Disclosure Letter 1.4 — "nothing admits… that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required"
This reservation is designed to neutralise the very issues flagged in sections 2–10. It's a disclosure letter, not an agreement, so it cannot itself limit our rights — but we should ensure the SPA warranties (consents obtained, no breach of material contracts, compliance with privacy law) are **not** undercut by it, and that these matters are addressed as conditions/indemnities.

---

## C. Specific unresolved items — these need conditions, price adjustment, or indemnities

### 9. Bluefen change-of-control consent (Clause 3/6.3; Disclosure §2) — MATERIAL
Bluefen is **~AUD 3.6m / ~30% of FY26 revenue** with a change-of-control clause (11.2) and conditions (11.3). The Seller admits **no final written consent** and no evidence conditions are satisfied. The Seller offers only "reasonable endeavours" and to treat consent as satisfied "on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Reasoning: Losing ~30% of revenue on change of control would materially impair the business we're paying AUD 24m for. "Reasonable endeavours" is a weak standard and the conditions in 11.3 may themselves be onerous.

**Push back:** Make a **clean, unconditional Bluefen consent a Condition Precedent to Completion** (not a post-completion best-efforts item), with the conditions in 11.3 satisfied. If the Seller won't make it a CP, require a **specific indemnity** for revenue loss / a price retention, and upgrade to "best endeavours."

### 10. Riverlark bank facility (Clause 2/7; Disclosure §3) — MATERIAL
**~AUD 3.2m outstanding**, change-of-control at 8.1, discharge at 9.2. Not repaid; no discharge of security included. Seller proposes a release "**following Completion**."

Reasoning: This is a **debt-free/cash-free deal**. AUD 3.2m of debt and, critically, **security over the company's assets** must be cleared **at or before Completion**, not afterwards. Accepting a post-completion release means we own a company with encumbered assets and rely on the Seller's promise.

**Push back:** 
- Full repayment/discharge of Riverlark and **release of all security as a Condition to Completion**, evidenced by a payoff/release letter delivered at Completion;
- The AUD 3.2m must be captured as **debt in the completion mechanism** / deducted from proceeds (funds flow). Confirm it is reflected, consistent with debt-free/cash-free.

### 11. DD-005 closing bonuses AUD 420,000 (Disclosure §5) — MATERIAL / funds-flow
The Seller says these bonuses are "a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow." But they are **conditional on Completion** and are a **company liability** triggered by the transaction.

Reasoning: On a debt-free/cash-free basis, Completion-triggered bonuses are properly a **Seller obligation / transaction cost** that should reduce proceeds or be borne by Seller — not a liability we inherit. Also note **payroll tax, superannuation and on-costs** may apply (disclosure is silent), increasing the true cost above AUD 420k.

**Push back:** Require the bonuses (plus all on-costs: super, payroll tax) to be either (a) paid by Seller pre-Completion, or (b) a specific indemnity / explicit deduction in the funds flow. They must not fall through to the buyer unpriced.

### 12. Ironquay IP / SOW3 (Clause 11.1; Disclosure §4) — MATERIAL IP RISK
DD-004 cl 7.3: transfer/assignment of **SOW3 Project Materials only occurs on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee**. DD-010 shows **AUD 180k open** (unverified). No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment in the data room. The Seller's indemnity is limited to "the specific SOW3 payment."

Reasoning: If SOW3 fees are unpaid, **we may not own the IP** in those Project Materials — the risk is not the AUD 180k payment, it's the **loss/encumbrance of IP rights** potentially core to the product. A AUD 180k-capped indemnity is inadequate to the real exposure.

**Push back:**
- Require **evidence of payment and a confirmatory written assignment** of all SOW3 Project Materials as a condition / pre-Completion deliverable;
- Reject the narrow indemnity cap — the indemnity should cover **loss arising from defective IP title**, not merely the fee amount, and sit **outside the general cap**;
- Add a specific **IP ownership warranty** on these materials.

### 13. Export/privacy incident (Clause 4.6/Sch 6; Disclosure §6) — MATERIAL / CONTINGENT
DD-006: a download link sent to an **unintended external address**, potentially **~1,240 records** (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps — personal information). Seller calls it "preliminary" and "not expected to be material," and the disclosure declines to characterise it as a breach or state loss.

Reasoning: This is a potential **eligible data breach** under the Privacy Act 1988 (Cth) Notifiable Data Breaches scheme. If notification is required and not made, there's regulatory exposure (OAIC), potential affected-individual claims, and reputational harm. "Not expected to be material" is the Seller's self-serving characterisation, not a risk assessment we can rely on.

**Push back:**
- Require the Seller to **complete the investigation** and confirm whether it is an eligible data breach / whether notification is required, before Completion;
- Obtain a **specific indemnity** for all losses, fines, remediation and notification costs arising from the incident, **uncapped by the general regime and not subject to the knowledge/disclosure defeats**;
- Add/confirm a **privacy & data-protection compliance warranty**. Do **not** let this be disclosed away under general disclosure.

### 14. Office lease notification (Disclosure §7) & Mossvale assignment restriction (§9)
Lower materiality but flag: DD-007 has a **notification obligation** (Seller argues it's not a consent requirement); DD-009 restricts assignment (Seller argues shares-sale doesn't trigger it). These are Seller characterisations. We should **independently verify** whether the share sale triggers any consent/notification and ensure a warranty that all required consents are/will be obtained, with any lease/key-contract consents added as CPs where material.

### 15. Sandbar supplier renewals — AUD 330k (Disclosure §8)
Three related renewals of AUD 110k each. Seller says "ordinary-course operating costs"; disclosure admits it **doesn't state whether they're unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course**. Read together they may be a single ~AUD 330k committed spend.

**Push back:** Clarify terms. If these are non-terminable committed costs incurred around signing, confirm treatment in the **leakage/ordinary-course warranty** and whether they belong in the completion accounts/net debt.

---

## D. Title & tax
- **Title (Disclosure §10):** Title is "evidenced by the share register at DD-012." A share register is **not conclusive proof of title** and the Seller notes we haven't verified. We should conduct our own verification and insist on a **full title warranty at 100% cap** (see item 1), plus stock transfer deliverables.
- **Tax (Seller Update):** The Seller wants tax "settled under the general regime." Reject — **tax should have its own covenant/indemnity with its own (longer) time limit** tied to the statutory period, outside the general cap.

---

## Summary of Recommendations (priority order)

**Deal-critical (Conditions Precedent / price):**
1. **Riverlark (AUD 3.2m):** full repayment + release of all security **as a CP**, with payoff letter at Completion; ensure captured as debt in funds flow (debt-free/cash-free).
2. **Bluefen (30% revenue):** clean unconditional consent **as a CP**; failing that, "best endeavours" + specific indemnity/retention for revenue loss.
3. **DD-005 bonuses (AUD 420k + on-costs):** Seller to bear — paid pre-Completion or deducted in funds flow; capture super/payroll tax.
4. **Ironquay SOW3 IP:** evidence of payment + confirmatory assignment pre-Completion; broad IP-loss indemnity outside the cap; add IP ownership warranty.
5. **Privacy incident (DD-006):** complete investigation + confirm NDB position pre-Completion; specific uncapped indemnity; privacy warranty; not subject to general disclosure.

**Liability architecture:**
6. Reject common cap/time-bar for **fundamental/title/capacity** warranties — separate them at **100% of price** with long (6–7 yr) limitation.
7. **Tax** carved out with its own indemnity and statutory-period time limit.
8. Reverse the "limitations apply to all Claims unless stated otherwise" default — limitations apply to **general warranties only**; specific indemnities, fundamentals, tax and **fraud** excluded.
9. Push general cap up from 20% (target 30–50%) and move to first-dollar basket recovery.
10. Exclude **fraud** from all caps, time limits, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses.

**Disclosure & knowledge:**
11. Replace "data room / public records" sweep-up with **fair disclosure** standard; reject general public-register disclosure.
12. Delete **constructive/"discoverable" knowledge** in Clause 8.3; limit to actual knowledge of named individuals (or seek pro-sandbagging). 
13. Treat the specific problem items (Bluefen, Riverlark, Ironquay, privacy) via **indemnities/CPs**, not disclosure, so they aren't defeated by §1.4 reservations or knowledge/disclosure defences.

**Verify/clarify:**
14. Independent **title verification** + transfer deliverables.
15. Confirm **lease notification and Mossvale** assignment don't require consent (don't accept Seller's bare characterisation); add consents as CPs if material.
16. Clarify **Sandbar renewals (AUD 330k)** — terminability, ordinary-course, and completion-accounts treatment.

---

Two cross-cutting observations worth keeping front of mind: first, the Seller has engineered a **mutually reinforcing set of limitations** (broad disclosure + constructive knowledge + "all Claims" default + exclusive remedy) that, if accepted together, would hollow out the warranty package — each needs to be pushed back individually. Second, the pattern on Bluefen, Riverlark, bonuses and SOW3 is the Seller trying to **defer or externalise known, quantified liabilities** to post-Completion or to the buyer; on a debt-free/cash-free deal these belong with the Seller or in the price.

Happy to turn this into a mark-up of the SPA clauses and a CP schedule, or draft the specific indemnities, on request.
